Multi-LLM Query Optimization

Arlen Dean Affiliation: Washington University in St. Louis, Olin Business School, arlen@wustl.edu    Zijin Zhang Affiliation: Boston College, Carroll School of Management, zijin.zhang@bc.edu    Stefanus Jasin Affiliation: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, sjasin@umich.edu    Yuqing Liu Affiliation: University of Michigan, Industrial and Operations Engineering, lyuqing@umich.edu
Abstract

Deploying multiple large language models (LLMs) in parallel to classify an unknown ground-truth label is a common practice, yet the problem of optimally allocating queries across heterogeneous models remains poorly understood. In this paper, we formulate a robust, offline query-planning problem that minimizes total query cost subject to statewise error constraints which guarantee reliability for every possible ground-truth label. We first establish that this problem is NP-hard via a reduction from the minimum-weight set cover problem. To overcome this intractability, we develop a surrogate by combining a union bound decomposition of the multi-class error into pairwise comparisons with Chernoff-type concentration bounds. The resulting surrogate admits a closed-form, multiplicatively separable expression in the query counts and is guaranteed to be feasibility-preserving. We further show that the surrogate is asymptotically tight at the optimization level: the ratio of surrogate-optimal cost to true optimal cost converges to one as error tolerances shrink, with an explicit rate of 𝒪⁡(log⁡log⁡(1/αmin)/log⁡(1/αmin))\mathcal{O}\left(\log\log(1/\alpha_{\min})/\log(1/\alpha_{\min})\right). Finally, we design an asymptotic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (AFPTAS) that returns a surrogate-feasible query plan within a (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon) factor of the surrogate optimum.

Keywords: large language models, query optimization, polynomial-time approximation

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming how organizations operate. Rather than relying on a single model, many deployments use a collection of LLMs and query them on the same task to aggregate their responses (Ai et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2025). Combining multiple predictors is well established in classical machine learning, where ensemble methods such as stacking can improve accuracy beyond any single learner (Wolpert 1992, Breiman 1996). However, the case for aggregation is especially compelling for LLMs because different models can disagree substantially due to differences in training data and architecture, and their outputs are inherently stochastic. Pooling across models and across repeated queries is therefore a natural mechanism for reducing this variability and improving reliability (Kuncheva and Whitaker 2003).

One prominent application of this multi-model approach is prediction, where a system consults several LLMs to infer an unknown ground-truth state from a finite set of outcomes. Such a use appears across many domains. In healthcare, a hospital system might run the same case through several diagnostic models and then aggregate their predicted diagnosis from a fixed menu of conditions (Yuan et al. 2026, More et al. 2026). In streaming or online marketplaces, platforms may combine outputs from multiple LLMs to classify customer intent into a finite set of content or product categories (Fang et al. 2024, Boateng et al. 2026). In legal services, document-review pipelines may route the same filing through several models and aggregate their labels for text classification (Huffman et al. 2025). In these settings, using multiple LLMs in parallel on the same unknown ground truth can yield substantial improvements over any single model.

Realizing these benefits in practice, however, is far from straightforward. Aggregating responses from multiple LLMs requires the decision maker to first determine how often to consult each model, based on their understanding of how each model performs across different categories of a given task. Yet each query consumes compute, adds latency, and incurs monetary cost through API fees or related charges (Shekhar et al. 2024). Querying all available models as many times as possible is therefore inefficient and wasteful, while querying too few may leave certain ground-truth labels poorly covered, resulting in unacceptable misclassification for those categories. Navigating between these extremes is difficult because models are heterogeneous in their discriminative power. A model that reliably distinguishes one pair of categories may be nearly uninformative for another, and repeated queries to the same model reduce uncertainty but with diminishing returns. Existing studies may offer partial guidance on individual model behavior, but they do not reveal how to distribute a limited budget across models whose strengths, weaknesses, and costs all interact. What is needed is an efficient allocation of queries across models, determined in advance, so that the aggregated responses are sufficient to reliably classify the unknown label. In practice, this allocation is largely handled through ad-hoc heuristics and trial-and-error. This gap motivates us to ask the following research questions:

  1. (i)

    How should a decision maker allocate queries across LLMs to minimize cost while guaranteeing a target level of accuracy across all possible ground-truth labels?

  2. (ii)

    How hard is this optimization problem, and how can we solve it tractably with provable guarantees?

1.1 Our Main Results and Contributions

Our main results and contributions are as follows:

A principled framework for offline multi-LLM query planning. We formulate a robust optimization model for the offline query-planning problem that arises whenever an organization consults multiple LLMs to classify an unknown state. The formulation captures three features that are central to practical deployments but have not been jointly addressed in the literature, namely (i) heterogeneous per-query costs across models, (ii) model-specific and state-dependent discriminative power, and (iii) statewise error constraints that require reliability for every possible ground-truth label, not just on average. The framework applies broadly to any firm that employs multiple LLMs for classification or prediction tasks and provides a rigorous foundation for the upstream planning decision of allocating a query budget across a heterogeneous collection of models.

NP-hardness and a tractable Chernoff surrogate. We establish that the query design problem is NP-hard via a reduction from the minimum-weight set cover problem (Theorem 1). The reduction exploits the fact that ensuring correct classification of every label forces the decision maker to select a collection of models whose combined discriminative reach spans all label pairs, at minimum total cost. To overcome this intractability, we develop a tractable surrogate that replaces each intractable statewise error constraint with an efficiently computable upper bound (Theorem 2). The construction proceeds in two steps. A union bound decomposes the multi-class probability error into pairwise label comparisons (Lemma 1), and a Chernoff exponential bound controls each pairwise term (Proposition 1). The resulting expression of the upper bound factorizes across models and query counts, which makes constraint evaluation efficient. Moreover, feasibility under the surrogate automatically implies feasibility under the original constraints.

Asymptotically Optimal Polynomial-time Approximation. We show that replacing the exact error constraints with the Chernoff surrogate does not significantly inflate the optimal query cost. Specifically, we prove that the ratio of surrogate-optimal cost to true optimal cost converges to one as the error tolerances shrink, with the excess vanishing at an explicit rate that is logarithmically smaller than the dominant cost scale (Theorem 3). The gap arises because the Chernoff proxy captures the correct exponential decay rate of each pairwise error probability but introduces a polynomial prefactor. Closing this prefactor requires only a negligible amount of additional query effort relative to the total budget any feasible plan must already spend. This result establishes that, in the high-reliability regime, solving the tractable surrogate yields essentially the same minimum cost as solving the intractable exact problem. The surrogate is therefore not merely a convenient analytical relaxation. It preserves the first-order cost structure that governs how query effort should be distributed across models. Building on this foundation, we design an asymptotic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (AFPTAS) that returns a surrogate-feasible query plan whose cost is within a factor of 1+ε1+\varepsilon of the surrogate optimum for any desired accuracy ε>0\varepsilon>0 (Theorem 4).

2 Literature Review

Multi-LLM systems.

A growing body of work studies how to combine or coordinate multiple LLMs to attain decision quality beyond that of any single model. The simplest aggregation strategy is majority voting, introduced in this setting through self-consistency decoding (Wang et al. 2022), where diverse chain-of-thought paths are sampled and the most frequent answer is selected. More sophisticated ensembling methods include pairwise ranking (Jiang et al. 2023) and approaches that exploit higher-order relationships across model outputs (Ai et al. 2025). For a recent survey, see Chen et al. (2025). A related paradigm is multi-agent debate, in which several models iteratively refine their answers through interaction (Du et al. 2024, Liang et al. 2023). Wang et al. (2025) study this idea through a mixture-of-agents architecture, while Li et al. (2024) examine how performance scales with the number of agents. A separate line of work considers per-query model selection rather than output aggregation. LLM routing methods assign each query to a single model to balance cost and quality (Ong et al. 2025, Ding et al. 2024), while LLM selects query models sequentially in order of increasing cost and stop once a confidence threshold is met (Chen et al. 2023, Jitkrittum et al. 2024, Gupta et al. 2024, Dekoninck et al. 2024). Across these studies, the focus is on how to aggregate or route outputs after they are observed. By contrast, our work addresses an upstream design problem: how many times to query each model before any outputs are collected, subject to cost and accuracy constraints.

Crowdsourcing and noisy label aggregation.

The problem of aggregating responses from multiple noisy sources to infer a latent ground truth has a long history in statistics and crowdsourcing. The foundational model of Dawid and Skene (1979) estimates annotator error rates via EM when the true label is unobserved. Our setting shares its core structure, with multiple sources that have heterogeneous accuracies, a latent class, and inference based on posterior maximization. Subsequent work extends this framework through richer classification models and alternative inference methods (Whitehill et al. 2009, Liu et al. 2012). On the algorithmic side, Zhang et al. (2014) develop spectral methods that improve on naive voting, while Raykar et al. (2010) study cost-quality tradeoffs in learning from crowd labels. Information-theoretic limits are also well understood. Gao et al. (2016) establish matching upper and lower bounds with an exact exponent characterized by average Chernoff information across workers, which parallels the role of pairwise Chernoff bounds in our surrogate construction. Moving from inference to budget allocation, Karger et al. (2011) and Karger et al. (2014) study budget-optimal non-adaptive task assignment in crowdsourcing. Their formulation is the closest structural antecedent to our problem. More broadly, the crowdsourcing literature typically assumes homogeneous query costs and considers assignment across many items. By contrast, we optimize integer query counts for a single classification instance with heterogeneous per-model costs, which results in a challenging combinatorial optimization problem.

Active Learning.

Our query-planning problem is also related to active learning, which studies how to select informative queries under budget constraints (Settles 2012). Much of this literature is adaptive, meaning that the learner observes each outcome before deciding what to query next. Classical examples include uncertainty sampling (Lewis and Gale 1994), query-by-committee (Seung et al. 1992), and variance-based statistical approaches (Cohn et al. 1996). These settings differ from ours because we require the decision maker to commit to a complete query plan before any outputs are observed. In this respect, our problem is closer to batch-mode active learning, which selects an entire set of queries in a single round (Hoi et al. 2006, Chen and Krause 2013, Zhang et al. 2024), and to cost-sensitive active learning with multiple imperfect oracles, where query decisions must account for heterogeneous costs and reliabilities (Donmez and Carbonell 2008, Yan et al. 2011). More broadly, this line of work connects to the classical literature on the value of information in hypothesis testing and sequential design (Chernoff 1952, Chernoff 1959). Within this broader perspective, our formulation belongs to a non-adaptive class of information acquisition problems such as controlled sensing (e.g., Nitinawarat et al. 2013), where non-adaptive observation policies can be asymptotically optimal for multihypothesis testing under fixed sample budgets .

3 Model and Preliminary Analysis

We consider a finite classification task in which a decision maker queries multiple large language models (LLMs) and aggregates their responses to predict an unknown ground-truth label. The unknown ground-truth label is a random variable, denoted by Y∈𝒴:={1,2,…,L}Y\in\mathcal{Y}:=\{1,2,\ldots,L\}, and the decision maker holds a strictly positive prior π⁡(y):=Pr⁡(Y=y)>0\pi(y):=\Pr(Y=y)>0 for every label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. To learn about the true label YY, the decision maker has access to KK different LLMs, indexed by m∈{1,…,K}m\in\{1,\ldots,K\}. A single query to model mm produces a random response Xm,t∈𝒳mX_{m,t}\in\mathcal{X}_{m} drawn from the conditional distribution pm​(x∣y):=Pr⁡(Xm,t=x∣Y=y)p_{m}(x\mid y):=\Pr(X_{m,t}=x\mid Y=y), where 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} represents the output alphabet of model mm and tt indexes repeated queries. For every model m∈{1,…,K}m\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, every label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, and every symbol x∈𝒳mx\in\mathcal{X}_{m}, we have pm​(x∣y)>0p_{m}(x\mid y)>0. Conditional on Y=yY=y, the outputs of each model are independent and identically distributed across repetitions, and outputs are mutually independent across models. The joint likelihood of all observed outputs therefore factorizes as

Pr({Xm,t=xm,t}m,t∣Y=y)=∏m=1K∏t=1rmpm(xm,t∣y),\Pr\bigl(\{X_{m,t}=x_{m,t}\}_{m,t}\mid Y=y\bigr)=\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}p_{m}(x_{m,t}\mid y), (1)

where rmr_{m} denotes the number of times that model mm is queried.

Our goal is to design a query plan, specified by a query-count vector r=(r1,…,rK)∈ℤ≥0Kr=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{K})\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}. The query plan is non-adaptive: the decision maker commits to a fixed number of queries per model before observing any outputs. Each query to model mm incurs a known cost cm>0c_{m}>0, and the total cost by a plan is denoted by C⁡(r):=∑m=1Kcm​rmC(r):=\sum_{m=1}^{K}c_{m}\,r_{m}. Once rr is fixed, the decision maker observes the dataset X(r):={Xm,t:1≤m≤K,1≤t≤rm}X(r):=\{X_{m,t}:1\leq m\leq K,1\leq t\leq r_{m}\}. Given the realized observations X⁡(r)=x⁡(r)X(r)=x(r), the decision maker updates their belief about the unknown ground-truth label YY using Bayes’ rule combined with the joint likelihood in (1). The posterior distribution of YY thus follows:

Pr⁡(Y=y∣X⁡(r)=x⁡(r))=π⁡(y)​∏m=1K∏t=1rmpm​(xm,t∣y)∑y′∈𝒴π⁡(y′)​∏m=1K∏t=1rmpm​(xm,t∣y′).\Pr\bigl(Y=y\mid X(r)=x(r)\bigr)=\frac{\pi(y)\;\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}p_{m}(x_{m,t}\mid y)}{\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi(y^{\prime})\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}p_{m}(x_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})}. (2)

The decision maker predicts label Y^\hat{Y} using the maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) rule, which selects the label with the largest posterior probability. Since the denominator in (2) does not depend on yy, maximizing the posterior probability is equivalent to solving

Y^r​(x⁡(r))∈arg​maxy∈𝒴⁡{π⁡(y)​∏m=1K∏t=1rmpm​(xm,t∣y)},\widehat{Y}_{r}\bigl(x(r)\bigr)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\Bigl\{\pi(y)\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}p_{m}(x_{m,t}\mid y)\Bigr\}, (3)

which we refer to as the MAP estimator. We evaluate the query performance through a statewise error probability

Pe​(y,r):=Pr⁡(Y^r​(X⁡(r))≠y∣Y=y),P_{e}(y;r):=\Pr(\widehat{Y}_{r}(X(r))\neq y\mid Y=y),

which measures the misclassification rate conditional on the true label being yy. This criterion is robust: it requires the error probability to be small for every possible ground-truth label, not just on average under a prior. Given a vector of target tolerances α=(αy)y∈𝒴∈(0,1)L\alpha=(\alpha_{y})_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\in(0,1)^{L}, the objective is to find the minimum-cost query plan satisfying every statewise constraint simultaneously:

minr∈ℤ≥0K\displaystyle\min_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}} C⁡(r)=∑m=1Kcm​rm\displaystyle C(r)=\sum_{m=1}^{K}c_{m}r_{m} (4)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} Pe(y;r)≤αy,∀y∈𝒴.\displaystyle P_{e}(y;r)\leq\alpha_{y},\qquad\forall y\in\mathcal{Y}.

Problem (4) is an integer program whose constraints couple the query counts through the combinatorial structure of the MAP error. To ensure that the problem is feasible for all sufficiently small tolerance vectors, we require that every pair of distinct labels be distinguishable by at least one model: for every label y≠y′y\neq y^{\prime}, there exists model mm with pm(⋅∣y)≠pm(⋅∣y′)p_{m}(\cdot\mid y)\neq p_{m}(\cdot\mid y^{\prime}). The remainder of this paper aims to develop an approach for designing cost-optimal query plans in this offline robust setting.

3.1 Hardness Result

Directly optimizing problem (4) is computationally intractable for two main reasons. First, the exact evaluation of Pe​(y,r)P_{e}(y;r) requires summing over all possible observation sequences, resulting in a combinatorial sum that grows exponentially in ∑i=1mri\sum_{i=1}^{m}r_{i} and is therefore infeasible to compute in general. Second, evaluating Pe​(y,r)P_{e}(y;r) also involves solving an inner nonlinear optimization problem to determine the estimator Y^r\hat{Y}_{r} within constraints. Taken together, these challenges make the problem difficult to solve exactly. We formally establish this computational difficulty by showing that the problem is NP-hard. For the remainder of the paper, all proofs are deferred to the Appendix.

Theorem 1 (NP-Hardness).

The query design problem (4) is NP-hard.

Theorem 1 shows that our optimization problem of solving the minimum-cost query plan is NP-hard. This can be proved by establishing a polynomial-time reduction from the minimum-weight set cover problem. The intuition is that each error constraint imposes a covering requirement: we can construct an instance such that for each potential ground-truth label to be correctly classified, at least one model that is capable of distinguishing it must be queried. Different models distinguish different subsets of labels, so the decision maker faces a combinatorial selection problem in choosing the cheapest collection of models whose discriminative capabilities jointly cover all labels. This is precisely the structure of the set cover problem, which is NP-hard. Therefore, no polynomial-time algorithm can solve the query design problem (4) exactly for all instances unless P = NP. To address this computational challenge, we next introduce a surrogate design approach.

4 Query Design: Surrogate Problem

A central challenge in multi-model query design is controlling the statewise classification error without explicitly computing posterior probabilities. As shown in Theorem 1, directly evaluating the statewise error probability Pe​(y,r)P_{e}(y;r) requires enumerating all possible observation sequences. When the number of queries grows, the number of such sequences increases exponentially, which makes exact evaluation computationally infeasible.

To overcome this difficulty, this section develops an analytically tractable upper bound on the statewise MAP error probabilities Pe​(y,r)P_{e}(y;r) by combining a union bound over pairwise comparisons with Chernoff bounding techniques. The resulting bound admits a closed-form expression and exhibits a key structural property: it decomposes multiplicatively across models and query counts. This separability allows us to transform the original query design problem into a more tractable optimization problem.

The key idea of our approach is to replace each intractable constraint Pe​(y,r)≤αyP_{e}(y;r)\leq\alpha_{y} with a tractable surrogate constraint P¯e​(y,r)≤αy\overline{P}_{e}(y;r)\leq\alpha_{y}, where P¯e​(y,r)\overline{P}_{e}(y;r) is constructed as a valid upper bound on the true error probability. Therefore, any query plan that satisfies the surrogate constraints automatically satisfies the original ones. At the same time, the surrogate bound admits a simple closed-form expression in terms of the query plan rr. This leads to the following optimization problem

minr∈ℤ≥0K\displaystyle\min_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}} C⁡(r)=∑m=1Kcm​rm\displaystyle C(r)=\sum_{m=1}^{K}c_{m}r_{m} (5)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} P¯e(y;r)≤αy,∀y∈𝒴.\displaystyle\overline{P}_{e}(y;r)\leq\alpha_{y},\qquad\forall y\in\mathcal{Y}.

Below, we construct P¯e​(y,r)\overline{P}_{e}(y;r) through a sequence of steps. We first decompose the MAP error event into pairwise comparisons between the true label and competing labels. We then bound each pairwise comparison probability using a Chernoff bound. Finally, combining these components yields a tractable upper bound that retains the essential statistical structure of the original problem.

4.1 Upper Bound Construction

The MAP rule selects the label whose posterior probability is largest. Equivalently, it selects the label that maximizes the posterior log-likelihood

Y^r​(x⁡(r))∈arg​maxy∈𝒴​log​π​(y)+∑m=1K∑t=1rmlog⁡pm​(xm,t∣y).\widehat{Y}_{r}\bigl(x(r)\bigr)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}~\log\pi(y)+\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{t=1}^{r_{m}}\log p_{m}(x_{m,t}\mid y).

An error occurs when some competing label y′y^{\prime} achieves a posterior log-likelihood at least as large as that of the true label yy. This observation motivates analyzing the classification error through a collection of pairwise comparisons between the true label and each competitor.

Definition 1 (Log-likelihood difference).

For any query plan r∈ℤ≥0Kr\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K} and distinct labels y,y′∈𝒴y,y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}, the log-likelihood difference is a random variable

Δy,y′​(r):=log⁡(π⁡(y′)π⁡(y))+∑m=1K∑t=1rmlog⁡(pm​(Xm,t∣y′)pm​(Xm,t∣y)).\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r):=\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime})}{\pi(y)}\right)+\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{t=1}^{r_{m}}\log\left(\frac{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})}{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)}\right). (6)

The quantity Δy,y′​(r)\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r) measures the advantage of the competing label y′y^{\prime} over the true label yy in terms of posterior log-likelihood. It consists of two components. The first term reflects the prior preference between the two labels, while the second term aggregates the evidence provided by the observed data. Each observation contributes a log-likelihood ratio comparing how likely that observation is under the two competing hypotheses. If the data is informative, this log-likelihood difference tends to favor the true label, causing Δy,y′​(r)\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r) to drift downward as more evidence is collected; otherwise, classification errors occur when the data incorrectly favors a competing label. Conditional on Y=yY=y, the event {Δy,y′(r)≥0}\{\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r)\geq 0\} indicates that a competing label is favored. Hence, the error event {Y^r(X(r))≠y}\{\hat{Y}_{r}(X(r))\neq y\} is contained in the union of events {Δy,y′(r)≥0}\{\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r)\geq 0\} over all competitors y′≠yy^{\prime}\neq y. This observation allows us to express the error event as a union of pairwise comparison events. The following lemma formalizes this reduction.

Lemma 1 (Union bound reduction to pairwise comparisons).

For any query plan r∈ℤ≥0Kr\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K} and label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

Pe​(y,r)≤∑y′∈𝒴∖{y}Pr⁡(Δy,y′​(r)≥0|Y=y).P_{e}(y;r)\leq\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{y\}}\Pr\big(\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r)\geq 0\,\big|\,Y=y\big). (7)

This lemma shows that the probability of misclassifying label yy can be controlled by bounding the probability that any competing label outperforms yy in terms of posterior log-likelihood. Conceptually, this step replaces a multi-class classification problem into a collection of binary tests. Each term in the sum corresponds to the probability that a particular competitor y′y^{\prime} beats the true label. This union bound provides a useful analytical simplification. Instead of analyzing the full multi-class error structure, we can focus on understanding the behavior of individual pairwise comparisons. However, the resulting probabilities are still difficult to compute exactly, because they depend on the enumeration of all possible observation sets. To obtain a tractable expression, we further bound these probabilities using a Chernoff parameter defined below.

Definition 2 (Chernoff affinity factor).

For any two distinct labels y,y′∈𝒴y,y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}, model m∈{1,…,K}m\in\{1,\dots,K\}, and tilting parameter s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1], we define the Chernoff affinity factor

Mm(y,y′)​(s):=∑x∈𝒳mpm​(x∣y) 1−s​pm​(x∣y′)s.M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)\;:=\;\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{m}}p_{m}(x\mid y)^{\,1-s}\;p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})^{\,s}. (8)

The Chernoff affinity factor measures the statistical overlap between the distributions induced by labels yy and y′y^{\prime} under model mm. When the two distributions are very similar, the value of Mm(y,y′)​(s)M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s) is close to one, reflecting the fact that observations from model mm provide little information for distinguishing the two labels. On the other hand, when the distributions are well separated, Mm(y,y′)​(s)M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s) becomes much smaller than one, indicating that the model is highly informative for this pairwise comparison.

From an operational perspective, this quantity captures the discriminative power of each model. It tells us how rapidly evidence accumulates in favor of the correct label when we collect observations from model mm. This interpretation will later play a key role in determining how query effort should be allocated across models. Using the Chernoff affinity factor, we can further bound the pairwise probability error in Proposition 1.

Proposition 1 (Pairwise Chernoff bound).

For any query vector r∈ℤ≥0Kr\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K} and distinct labels y,y′∈𝒴y,y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y},

Pr⁡(Δy,y′​(r)≥0|Y=y)≤mins∈[0,1]⁡(π⁡(y′)π⁡(y))s​∏m=1K(Mm(y,y′)​(s))rm.\Pr\!\big(\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r)\geq 0\,\big|\,Y=y\big)\leq\min_{s\in[0,1]}\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime})}{\pi(y)}\right)^{s}\prod_{m=1}^{K}\big(M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)\big)^{r_{m}}. (9)

Proposition 1 provides the key analytical tool that allows tractable error control. The Chernoff bound transforms the error probability based on the log-likelihood difference and observation sets into an exponential bound that depends only on the query counts. Two structural properties are particularly important. First, the bound factorizes across models: each model contributes a term (Mm(y,y′)​(s))rm(M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s))^{r_{m}}. Second, each of these terms decays exponentially with the number of queries rmr_{m}. Intuitively, every additional observation from an informative model reduces the probability that the competing label can accumulate sufficient evidence to beat the true label. Besides, the parameter ss acts as an exponential tilting parameter that optimally balances the contributions of the two competing distributions. Optimizing over ss selects the tightest exponential bound for each pairwise comparison. Combining Lemmas 1 and 1 leads to the following upper bound on the statewise classification error.

Theorem 2 (Statewise Error Upper Bound).

For any query plan r∈ℤ≥0Kr\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K} and label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

Pe​(y,r)≤P¯e​(y,r):=∑y′∈𝒴∖{y}mins∈[0,1]⁡(π⁡(y′)π⁡(y))s​∏m=1K(Mm(y,y′)​(s))rm.P_{e}(y;r)\leq\overline{P}_{e}(y;r):=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{y\}}\min_{s\in[0,1]}\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime})}{\pi(y)}\right)^{s}\prod_{m=1}^{K}\big(M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)\big)^{r_{m}}. (10)

This result provides a tractable surrogate for the otherwise intractable statewise error probability. Beyond its analytical convenience, the bound also offers useful insights into how query effort affects classification accuracy.

First, the bound exhibits a separable structure in the query vector rr. For any fixed pair (y,y′)(y,y^{\prime}) and tilting parameter ss, the expression consists of a product of terms (Mm(y,y′)​(s))rm(M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s))^{r_{m}}, each corresponding to one model. This means that every additional query from model mm contributes a fixed amount of evidence toward correct classification, i.e., a multiplicative reduction in the probability that the competing label y′y^{\prime} can overtake the true label yy. This separable structure is exactly what makes the surrogate problem (5) efficient: the effect of querying each model can be evaluated independently and aggregated through simple additive contributions.

Second, the bound provides a natural interpretation of model informativeness. The quantity Mm(y,y′)​(s)M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s) captures the statistical overlap between the two distributions associated with labels yy and y′y^{\prime} under model mm. When the two distributions are very similar, the overlap is close to one, meaning that observations from this model provide little evidence for distinguishing the two labels. In contrast, when the distributions are well separated, the overlap is small, and each observation from that model quickly reduces the probability of confusion between yy and y′y^{\prime}. As a result, models that are more informative for distinguishing specific label pairs will contribute larger reductions in the bound, and an optimal query strategy will naturally allocate more queries to such models.

Finally, the bound highlights the role of prior information. The factor (π⁡(y′)/π⁡(y))s(\pi(y^{\prime})/\pi(y))^{s} reflects the initial advantage that one label may have over another before any data is observed. When the true label yy has a higher prior probability, the classifier begins with a favorable bias, so less observational evidence is needed to maintain correct classification. However, when the competing label y′y^{\prime} has a stronger prior, additional observations must compensate for this disadvantage. In this sense, the bound explicitly captures the interplay between prior beliefs and the information obtained from data.

Taken together, these properties explain why the bound is well suited for query design. Although it replaces the exact error probability with an upper bound, it preserves the key statistical properties that guide the learning process: prior information, the discriminative power of each model, and the cumulative effect of additional observations. At the same time, its separable structure allows efficient optimization over the query plan rr and makes it a practical tool for designing cost-effective data collection strategies.

4.2 Tightness of Optimization Decisions

The previous subsection establishes that the surrogate error probability P¯e​(y,r)\overline{P}_{e}(y;r) is a valid upper bound on the true MAP error Pe​(y,r)P_{e}(y;r). This guarantees that the surrogate problem is feasibility-preserving, but it does not by itself answer the more relevant design question: does the surrogate significantly change the optimal query plan? We note that, for our purposes, the natural notion of tightness is decision-based rather than pointwise. To make this precise, we compare the minimum costs achievable under the exact and surrogate problems.

We fix a vector of error tolerances α=(αy)y∈𝒴∈(0,1)L\alpha=(\alpha_{y})_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\in(0,1)^{L} and define the true and surrogate feasible sets

ℛ⁡(α)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\alpha) :={r∈ℤ≥0K:Pe(y;r)≤αyfor all y∈𝒴},ℛ¯(α):={r∈ℤ≥0K:P¯e(y;r)≤αyfor all y∈𝒴}.\displaystyle:=\Big\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}:P_{e}(y;r)\leq\alpha_{y}\ \text{for all }y\in\mathcal{Y}\Big\},\ \overline{\mathcal{R}}(\alpha):=\Big\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}:\overline{P}_{e}(y;r)\leq\alpha_{y}\ \text{for all }y\in\mathcal{Y}\Big\}.

Using these feasible sets, we can define the optimal costs associated with each formulation.

Definition 3 (Optimal costs).

The true and surrogate optimal costs are

OPT⁡(α):=minr∈ℛ⁡(α)⁡C⁡(r),OPT¯​(α):=minr∈ℛ¯​(α)⁡C⁡(r),\mathrm{OPT}(\alpha):=\min_{r\in\mathcal{R}(\alpha)}C(r),\qquad\overline{\mathrm{OPT}}(\alpha):=\min_{r\in\overline{\mathcal{R}}(\alpha)}C(r),

with the convention min⁡∅:=+∞\min\emptyset:=+\infty.

Whenever the relevant feasible set is nonempty, the corresponding minimum is attained because cm>0c_{m}>0 for every mm and each cost sublevel set {r∈ℤ≥0K:C⁡(r)≤c}\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}:C(r)\leq c\} is finite. Moreover, the statewise Chernoff bound in Theorem 2 implies the inclusion ℛ¯​(α)⊆ℛ​(α)\overline{\mathcal{R}}(\alpha)\subseteq\mathcal{R}(\alpha), and hence the following result.

Corollary 1 (Surrogate conservatism).

For every tolerance vector α∈(0,1)L\alpha\in(0,1)^{L},

OPT​(α)≤OPT¯​(α).\mathrm{OPT}(\alpha)\leq\overline{\mathrm{OPT}}(\alpha).

Corollary 1 suggests that the surrogate problem is conservative. We point out that since the surrogate bound P¯e​(y,r)\overline{P}_{e}(y;r) is obtained by combining a union bound across competing labels with pairwise Chernoff bounds, the gap between the true error Pe​(y,r)P_{e}(y;r) and the surrogate P¯e​(y,r)\overline{P}_{e}(y;r) at a fixed query vector rr is not the most informative metric. What matters in practice is whether replacing the exact constraints by the surrogate changes the optimal cost OPT⁡(α)\mathrm{OPT}(\alpha) required to achieve the prescribed error tolerances.

To state our main result in this section, we impose one mild regularity condition beyond the standing assumptions of Section 3. We require that the log-likelihood ratios are uniformly bounded, that is, there exists B<∞B<\infty such that

|log⁡(pm​(x∣y′)pm​(x∣y))|≤Bfor all ​m,y≠y′,x∈𝒳m.\left|\log\left(\frac{p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})}{p_{m}(x\mid y)}\right)\right|\leq B\qquad\text{for all }m,\ y\neq y^{\prime},\ x\in\mathcal{X}_{m}.

This condition is standard in finite-alphabet settings and, together with the assumption that every label pair is distinguishable by at least one model, rules out degenerate cases in which a small number of observations can dominate the comparison between two labels. Let αmin:=miny∈𝒴⁡αy\alpha_{\min}:=\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\alpha_{y} denote the smallest error tolerance. The following result shows that the additional cost from using the surrogate vanishes as αmin\alpha_{\min} approaches 0.

Theorem 3 (Optimization-level tightness).

Suppose the uniform boundedness condition above is satisfied. Then for all sufficiently small αmin\alpha_{\min}, if OPT⁡(α)<∞\mathrm{OPT}(\alpha)<\infty,

1≤OPT¯​(α)OPT⁡(α)≤1+O⁡(log⁡log⁡(1/αmin)log⁡(1/αmin)).1\leq\frac{\overline{\mathrm{OPT}}(\alpha)}{\mathrm{OPT}(\alpha)}\leq 1+O\!\left(\frac{\log\log\!\left(1/\alpha_{\min}\right)}{\log\!\left(1/\alpha_{\min}\right)}\right).

In particular, this ratio approaches 11 as αmin→0\alpha_{\min}\to 0.

The tightness result in Theorem 3 shows that the Chernoff surrogate is asymptotically exact at the optimization level. Although the surrogate may exclude some query plans that are feasible for the original problem, the resulting increase in the optimal cost OPT⁡(α)\mathrm{OPT}(\alpha) is negligible relative to the true optimum once the error tolerances become sufficiently small. In other words, in the high-reliability regime, solving the tractable surrogate problem yields essentially the same minimum cost as solving the intractable exact problem.

The threshold for how small αmin\alpha_{\min} should be is a problem-dependent constant, determined by the prior, the log-likelihood bound BB, cost structure, and the Chernoff affinity factors, but not by the tolerance vector α\alpha itself. It delineates the high-reliability regime in which OPT⁡(α)\mathrm{OPT}(\alpha) is large enough (of order log⁡(1/αmin)\log(1/\alpha_{\min})) for the additive padding cost to become negligible. For any concrete instance, this threshold can in principle be computed from the model parameters. In practice, the requirement of αmin\alpha_{\min} being sufficiently small is mild, since the regime of interest is precisely when error tolerances are not big.

The proof hinges on two observations. First, for each label pair (y,y′)(y,y^{\prime}), the optimized Chernoff proxy matches the true pairwise comparison probability up to a sub-exponential factor of order 1/n1/\sqrt{n}, where nn is the number of queries allocated to models that actually distinguish yy from y′y^{\prime}. Thus the surrogate captures the correct exponential decay rate of the error and loses only a polynomial prefactor. Second, this remaining gap can be removed with very little additional query effort. Specifically, each additional round of queries to every model shrinks each pairwise Chernoff term by a fixed factor ϑ∈(0,1)\vartheta\in(0,1) (see Lemma 9). Since any plan that is optimal for the original problem already requires total query effort of order log⁡(1/αmin)\log(1/\alpha_{\min}), only O⁡(log⁡log⁡(1/αmin))O(\log\log(1/\alpha_{\min})) additional rounds are needed to absorb the polynomial prefactor and allow the plan feasible for the surrogate. This produces a lower-order additive cost, which is precisely what drives the cost ratio in Theorem 3 to one.

We note that the practical implication is significant. The surrogate is not just a convenient analytical relaxation. It preserves the first-order cost trade-off that controls how query effort should be distributed across models. This observation makes the upper bound construction in Section 4.1 appropriate not only for proving feasibility, but also for guiding the actual query design. The next subsection leverages this structure to describe how the surrogate problem can be solved computationally.

4.3 Approximation Scheme for the Surrogate Problem

This section develops an approximation algorithm for the surrogate problem (5). The constraint in (5) involves P¯e​(y,r)\overline{P}_{e}(y;r), which itself contains a minimization problem over the Chernoff parameter s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1] for each pairwise term. In what next, we provide a reformulation of the surrogate problem which removes the inner minimization over parameter ss. The following proposition shows that this is possible without any loss of optimality or feasibility.

Proposition 2 (Reformulation).

Let 𝒫={(y,y′)∈𝒴2:y≠y′}\mathcal{P}=\{(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Y}^{2}:y\neq y^{\prime}\} denote the set of ordered pairs. The surrogate problem (5) is equivalent to the joint problem

minr∈ℤ≥0K,s=(s(y,y′))(y,y′)∈𝒫∈[0,1]|𝒫|\displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K},\\[2.0pt] s\,=\,(s_{(y,y^{\prime})})_{(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}}\,\in\,[0,1]^{|\mathcal{P}|}\end{subarray}} C⁡(r)\displaystyle C(r) (11)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ∑y′≠y(π⁡(y′)π⁡(y))s(y,y′)∏m=1K(Mm(y,y′)(s(y,y′)))rm≤αy,∀y∈𝒴.\displaystyle\sum_{y^{\prime}\neq y}\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime})}{\pi(y)}\right)^{\!s_{(y,y^{\prime})}}\prod_{m=1}^{K}\!\bigl(M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s_{(y,y^{\prime})})\bigr)^{r_{m}}\;\leq\;\alpha_{y},\qquad\forall\,y\in\mathcal{Y}.

Proposition 2 brings two benefits. First, feasibility becomes log-linear in rr for fixed ss: with ss held constant, each constraint in (11) reduces to a sum of exponentials that are log-linear in rr, leading to a convex and separable subproblem amenable to standard solvers. Second, the tilting parameters s(y,y′)s_{(y,y^{\prime})} are now explicit decision variables on the compact domain [0,1]|𝒫|[0,1]^{|\mathcal{P}|}, which opens the door to discretisation: approximating this domain with a finite grid of resolution δ\delta reduces the problem to a finite collection of integer subproblems, each with fixed ss.

Based on this formulation, we next propose an algorithm that solves the surrogate problem efficiently. This algorithm follows asymptotic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (AFPTAS).

 

Algorithm 1 AFPTAS for the Chernoff Surrogate Design Problem

 
1: Input: (K,𝒴,𝒫,{Mm(y,y′)},{cm},π,α)(K,\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{P},\{M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}\},\{c_{m}\},\pi,\alpha), accuracy ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1], query-count bound NmaxN_{\max}, scale parameter Λ\Lambda
2: Output: surrogate-feasible design r^∈ℤ≥0K\widehat{r}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}
3: Set grid mesh h←log⁡(1+ε)/Λh\leftarrow\log(1+\varepsilon)/\Lambda
4: Build ss-grid 𝒢ε←{0,h,2​h,…,⌊1/h⌋​h,1}|𝒫|\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}\leftarrow\{0,h,2h,\dots,\lfloor 1/h\rfloor h,1\}^{|\mathcal{P}|}
5: for each grid point s∈𝒢εs\in\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon} do
6:  Set rounding scale Δ←log⁡(1+ε)/Nmax\Delta\leftarrow\log(1+\varepsilon)/N_{\max} and state-space cutoff Tmax←⌈B​Nmax/Δ⌉T_{\max}\leftarrow\lceil BN_{\max}/\Delta\rceil
7:  for m=1,…,Km=1,\dots,K, p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} do
8:   Round discrimination weight w~m,p(s)←⌊−logMm(y,y′)(sp)/Δ⌋\widetilde{w}_{m,p}(s)\leftarrow\left\lfloor-\log M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s_{p})/\Delta\right\rfloor
9:  end for
10:  DP⁡[𝟎]←0\mathrm{DP}[\mathbf{0}]\leftarrow 0
11:  for t∈{0,…,Tmax}|𝒫|t\in\{0,\dots,T_{\max}\}^{|\mathcal{P}|} in non-decreasing ‖t‖1\|t\|_{1} order do
12:   DP⁡[t]←minm⁡{cm+DP⁡[(t−w~m)+]}\mathrm{DP}[t]\leftarrow\min_{m}\{c_{m}+\mathrm{DP}[(t-\widetilde{w}_{m})_{+}]\}
13:  end for
14:  Find cheapest feasible state t†(s)←argmin{DP[t]:∑y′≠y(π⁡(y′)π⁡(y))spe−Δ​tp≤αy,∀y∈𝒴}t^{\dagger}(s)\leftarrow\arg\min\{\mathrm{DP}[t]:\sum_{y^{\prime}\neq y}\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime})}{\pi(y)}\right)^{s_{p}}e^{-\Delta t_{p}}\leq\alpha_{y},\ \forall y\in\mathcal{Y}\}
15:  Recover design r†​(s)r^{\dagger}(s) by backtracking from t†​(s)t^{\dagger}(s)
16: end for
17: r^←arg⁡mins∈𝒢ε⁡C⁡(r†​(s))\widehat{r}\leftarrow\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}}C(r^{\dagger}(s))
18: return r^\widehat{r}
 

Algorithm 4.3 proceeds in two stages. In the first stage, it discretises the continuous tilting parameter s∈[0,1]|𝒫|s\in[0,1]^{|\mathcal{P}|} into a finite ss-grid 𝒢ε\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon} by setting a mesh h=log⁡(1+ε)/Λh=\log(1+\varepsilon)/\Lambda, where Λ\Lambda is a scale parameter controlling how fast the pairwise Chernoff bound changes as ss varies. The mesh is calibrated so that adjusting any tilting parameter to the nearest grid point inflates each pairwise error bound by at most a factor of (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon). In the second stage, the algorithm iterates over every grid point s∈𝒢εs\in\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon} and runs a fixed-ss dynamic program. At each grid point, the discrimination weights wm,p​(s)=−log⁡Mm(y,y′)​(sp)w_{m,p}(s)=-\log M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s_{p}) are rounded down to integer multiples of the rounding scale Δ=log⁡(1+ε)/Nmax\Delta=\log(1+\varepsilon)/N_{\max}, which produce integer weights w~m,p​(s)\widetilde{w}_{m,p}(s). Rounding down is conservative: it understates how much each query discriminates, so any design the DP allows feasible remains feasible under the exact weights. The DP itself is an unbounded-knapsack recursion over states t∈{0,…,Tmax}|𝒫|t\in\{0,\ldots,T_{\max}\}^{|\mathcal{P}|}, where DP⁡[t]\mathrm{DP}[t] records the minimum cost to accumulate at least tpt_{p} rounded discrimination units for every pair pp. The cheapest state whose associated conservative error bound ∑y′≠y(π⁡(y′)π⁡(y))sp​e−Δ​tp\sum_{y^{\prime}\neq y}\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime})}{\pi(y)}\right)^{s_{p}}e^{-\Delta t_{p}} satisfies all constraints is selected as t†​(s)t^{\dagger}(s), and the corresponding integer design r†​(s)r^{\dagger}(s) is recovered by backtracking. The algorithm finally returns the cheapest design across all grid points.

Theorem 4 (AFPTAS guarantee).

The design r^\widehat{r} returned by Algorithm 4.3 is surrogate-feasible, and for sufficiently small αmin\alpha_{\min}, the multiplicative guarantee

C⁡(r^)≤(1+ε)​OPT¯​(α)C(\widehat{r})\;\leq\;(1+\varepsilon)\,\overline{\mathrm{OPT}}(\alpha) (12)

holds. Algorithm 4.3 is polynomial in KK, log⁡(1/αmin)\log(1/\alpha_{\min}), and 1/ε1/\varepsilon for fixed LL.

Theorem 4 follows from the discretization and conservative rounding in the two stages of Algorithm Section 4.3. First, discretizing the Chernoff tilting parameters onto the grid 𝒢​ε\mathcal{G}\varepsilon allows that replacing any optimal tilting vector by its nearest grid point increases each pairwise Chernoff bound by at most a multiplicative factor (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon). Second, the dynamic program uses rounded-down discrimination weights, which makes the feasibility check conservative: the rounded weights underestimate the true discrimination power of each query, so any design that is feasible by the DP also satisfies the original surrogate constraints. This rounding introduces only a bounded additive loss in the accumulated discrimination levels. When the minimum error tolerance αmin\alpha_{\min} is sufficiently small, the optimal cost necessarily scales at least logarithmically with 1/αmin1/\alpha_{\min}. As a result, the additive loss becomes negligible relative to the optimal objective value, leading to the multiplicative guarantee C⁡(r^)≤(1+ε)​OPT¯​(α)C(\widehat{r})\leq(1+\varepsilon)\overline{\mathrm{OPT}}(\alpha). Overall, Algorithm 4.3 constitutes an asymptotic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: although the (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon) approximation ratio is not uniform across all parameter regimes, it holds in the practically relevant small-tolerance regime while the running time remains polynomial in KK, log⁡(1/αmin)\log(1/\alpha_{\min}), and 1/ε1/\varepsilon for fixed LL.

5 Conclusion

This paper addresses the problem of allocating queries across multiple heterogeneous LLMs to classify an unknown label at minimum cost while meeting label-specific accuracy guarantees. Three main contributions emerge from the analysis. First, the query design problem is NP-hard, and the source of hardness is the combinatorial interaction between per-model costs and the requirement that every ground-truth label should be reliably covered. Second, a Chernoff-based surrogate relaxation makes the problem tractable without meaningfully inflating the optimal cost. The surrogate-to-true cost ratio vanishes at rate 𝒪⁡(log⁡log⁡(1/αmin)/log⁡(1/αmin))\mathcal{O}(\log\log(1/\alpha_{\min})/\log(1/\alpha_{\min})), confirming that the relaxation preserves the economically relevant structure of the original problem when error tolerances are small. Third, an asymptotic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme solves the surrogate to within a (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon) factor of the surrogate optimum.

Taken together, these results provide an alternative to the ad-hoc heuristics that currently govern multi-LLM query allocation. Models differ in their per-query costs and in their ability to distinguish specific label pairs, making the optimal allocation fundamentally combinatorial. Our framework shows that this difficulty can be overcome through a surrogate whose optimal plans are near-optimal for the original and can be computed efficiently. The formulation applies broadly to any setting where multiple stochastic classifiers are queried on a shared unknown state, including medical diagnosis, content categorization, and document review.

Appendix A Proofs for Section 3

This appendix collects the proofs of all results stated in Section 3.

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof of Theorem 1.

We reduce from Minimum-Weight Set Cover, which is NP-hard (Karp 2009). An instance consists of a universe U={1,…,n}U=\{1,\ldots,n\}, sets S1,…,SK⊆US_{1},\ldots,S_{K}\subseteq U with ⋃j=1KSj=U\bigcup_{j=1}^{K}S_{j}=U, positive weights w1,…,wK>0w_{1},\ldots,w_{K}>0, and a budget BSC>0B_{\mathrm{SC}}>0. The question is whether a sub-collection of total weight at most BSCB_{\mathrm{SC}} can cover UU.

Construction. Given such an instance, we build a query-plan instance as follows. Set L=n+1L=n+1 and 𝒴={0,1,…,n}\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}, where label 00 is a “null” confuser and labels 1,…,n1,\ldots,n correspond to universe elements. Define the prior

π(0)=12,π(i)=12​n,i=1,…,n.\pi(0)=\frac{1}{2},\qquad\pi(i)=\frac{1}{2n},\quad i=1,\ldots,n. (13)

Introduce a discriminator model m∗m^{*} with output alphabet {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}, cost cm∗=δ′>0c_{m^{*}}=\delta^{\prime}>0 (negligibly small), and conditional distributions

pm∗​(x∣y)={𝟏[x=i],y=i≥1,1n,y=0.p_{m^{*}}(x\mid y)=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}[x=i],&y=i\geq 1,\\ \frac{1}{n},&y=0.\end{cases} (14)

For each set SjS_{j}, introduce a set-cover model jj with binary output alphabet {0,1}\{0,1\}, cost cj=wjc_{j}=w_{j}, and, for a fixed ε∈(0,14)\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac{1}{4}),

pj​(x∣y)={12,y=0,(1−ε)𝟏[x=1]ε𝟏[x=0],y=i≥1​ and ​i∈Sj,12,y=i≥1​ and ​i∉Sj.p_{j}(x\mid y)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2},&y=0,\\ (1-\varepsilon)^{\mathbf{1}[x=1]}\,\varepsilon^{\mathbf{1}[x=0]},&y=i\geq 1\text{ and }i\in S_{j},\\ \frac{1}{2},&y=i\geq 1\text{ and }i\notin S_{j}.\end{cases} (15)

In words, when i∈Sji\in S_{j}, model jj outputs 11 with probability 1−ε1-\varepsilon and 00 with probability ε\varepsilon. Otherwise, it outputs each value with probability 1/21/2, identically to its behavior under label 00. Set tolerances α0=1−δ′′\alpha_{0}=1-\delta^{\prime\prime} (nearly trivial, for small δ′′>0\delta^{\prime\prime}>0) and αi=2​ε\alpha_{i}=2\varepsilon for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, and budget B=BSC+δ′B=B_{\mathrm{SC}}+\delta^{\prime}.

Error analysis. We show that the error constraints are equivalent to the covering requirement. Any cost-optimal plan includes model m∗m^{*} exactly once, since its cost is negligible and it is necessary for separating non-null labels from one another. Fix the true label Y=iY=i for some i≥1i\geq 1, and suppose rm∗=1r_{m^{*}}=1. Since pm∗(i∣j)=𝟏[i=j]=0p_{m^{*}}(i\mid j)=\mathbf{1}[i=j]=0 for j≥1j\geq 1, j≠ij\neq i, the observation Xm∗,1=iX_{m^{*},1}=i drives all non-null posteriors other than Pr⁡(Y=i∣Xm∗,1=i)\Pr(Y=i\mid X_{m^{*},1}=i) to zero, i.e., the posterior Pr⁡(Y=k∣Xm∗,1=i)=0\Pr(Y=k\mid X_{m^{*},1}=i)=0 for every non-null label k≠ik\neq i. The log-posterior-odds between labels 00 and ii are then

log⁡π⁡(0)​pm∗​(i∣0)π⁡(i)​pm∗​(i∣i)=log⁡12⋅1n12​n⋅1=0,\log\frac{\pi(0)\,p_{m^{*}}(i\mid 0)}{\pi(i)\,p_{m^{*}}(i\mid i)}=\log\frac{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{n}}{\frac{1}{2n}\cdot 1}=0,

so after model m∗m^{*} the MAP decision reduces to a binary comparison between labels ii and 00 starting from a perfect tie.

By inspection of (15), if i∉Sji\notin S_{j} then pj(⋅∣i)=pj(⋅∣0)=(1/2,1/2)p_{j}(\cdot\mid i)=p_{j}(\cdot\mid 0)=(1/2,1/2), so model jj yields log-likelihood ratio zero for every observation and is entirely uninformative for breaking this tie. If instead i∈Sji\in S_{j}, the per-observation log-likelihood ratio is

Λj​(X):=log⁡pj​(X∣i)pj​(X∣0)={log⁡(2​(1−ε))>0,X=1,log⁡(2​ε)<0,X=0.\Lambda_{j}(X):=\log\frac{p_{j}(X\mid i)}{p_{j}(X\mid 0)}=\begin{cases}\log\bigl(2(1-\varepsilon)\bigr)>0,&X=1,\\[4.0pt] \log(2\varepsilon)<0,&X=0.\end{cases}

The cumulative log-posterior-odds after all queries are therefore

Λtotal=0⏟after ​m∗+∑j:i∈Sjrj≥1∑t=1rjΛj(Xj,t)+∑j:i∉Sjrj≥1∑t=1rj0⏟= 0.\Lambda_{\mathrm{total}}=\underbrace{0}_{\text{after }m^{*}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j:\,i\in S_{j}\\ r_{j}\geq 1\end{subarray}}\sum_{t=1}^{r_{j}}\Lambda_{j}(X_{j,t})+\underbrace{\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j:\,i\notin S_{j}\\ r_{j}\geq 1\end{subarray}}\sum_{t=1}^{r_{j}}0}_{=\,0}.

Suppose there exists jj with i∈Sji\in S_{j} and rj≥1r_{j}\geq 1. A misclassification requires Λtotal≤0\Lambda_{\mathrm{total}}\leq 0. With a single covering query,

Pe​(i,r)≤Pr⁡(Λj​(Xj,1)≤0∣Y=i)=Pr⁡(Xj,1=0∣Y=i)=ε<2​ε=αi.P_{e}(i;\,r)\leq\Pr\!\bigl(\Lambda_{j}(X_{j,1})\leq 0\mid Y=i\bigr)=\Pr(X_{j,1}=0\mid Y=i)=\varepsilon<2\varepsilon=\alpha_{i}.

Additional covering queries can only decrease Pe​(i,r)P_{e}(i;\,r), since each contributes a strictly positive expected log-likelihood ratio favoring the correct label. Now suppose instead that rj=0r_{j}=0 for every jj with i∈Sji\in S_{j}. Every queried set-cover model satisfies i∉Sji\notin S_{j}, so Λtotal=0\Lambda_{\mathrm{total}}=0 for every realization of X⁡(r)X(r), and labels ii and 00 have identical posteriors regardless of the data. Any deterministic tie-breaking rule that does not uniformly favor label ii yields Pe​(i,r)=1>2​εP_{e}(i;\,r)=1>2\varepsilon; the best randomized rule (uniform) yields Pe​(i,r)=1/2>2​εP_{e}(i;\,r)=1/2>2\varepsilon since ε<1/4\varepsilon<1/4. Combining both directions: the statewise constraint Pe​(i,r)≤2​εP_{e}(i;\,r)\leq 2\varepsilon holds for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n if and only if 𝒞⁡(r):={j:rj≥1}\mathcal{C}(r):=\{j:r_{j}\geq 1\} covers UU.

Cost equivalence.  Given a set cover 𝒞∗\mathcal{C}^{*} with ∑j∈𝒞∗wj≤BSC\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}^{*}}w_{j}\leq B_{\mathrm{SC}}, define rj=𝟏[j∈𝒞∗]r_{j}=\mathbf{1}[j\in\mathcal{C}^{*}] and rm∗=1r_{m^{*}}=1. This plan is feasible by the above equivalence and has cost C⁡(r)=δ′+∑j∈𝒞∗wj≤BC(r)=\delta^{\prime}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}^{*}}w_{j}\leq B. By contrast, given a feasible plan rr with C⁡(r)≤BC(r)\leq B, we may assume without loss of generality that rj∈{0,1}r_{j}\in\{0,1\} for each set-cover model (additional queries only increase cost without avoiding feasibility), so 𝒞⁡(r)\mathcal{C}(r) is a valid cover with ∑j∈𝒞⁡(r)wj=C⁡(r)−δ′≤BSC\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}(r)}w_{j}=C(r)-\delta^{\prime}\leq B_{\mathrm{SC}}.

The construction is polynomial-time and the two decision problems have identical yes/no answers, so NP-hardness of Minimum-Weight Set Cover implies NP-hardness of the decision problem (4). ∎

Appendix B Proofs for Section 4

This appendix collects the proofs of all results stated in Section 4.

B.1 Proof of Lemma 1

Proof of Lemma 1.

MAP rule as posterior likelihood maximization. By assumption, all likelihoods are strictly positive, and π⁡(a)>0\pi(a)>0 for all aa. Therefore the posterior quantity

π⁡(a)​∏m=1K∏t=1rmpm​(xm,t∣a)\pi(a)\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}p_{m}(x_{m,t}\mid a)

is strictly positive for every aa and every realization x⁡(r)x(r). Since the logarithm is strictly increasing, maximizing the posterior probability is equivalent to maximizing the posterior log-likelihood, and thus

Y^r​(x⁡(r))∈arg⁡maxa∈𝒴​[log⁡π⁡(a)+∑m=1K∑t=1rmlog⁡pm​(xm,t∣a)].\widehat{Y}_{r}(x(r))\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{Y}}\left[\log\pi(a)+\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{t=1}^{r_{m}}\log p_{m}(x_{m,t}\mid a)\right].

Error event. Fix the ground-truth label yy and define the error event

ℰy={Y^r(X(r))≠y}.\mathcal{E}_{y}=\{\widehat{Y}_{r}(X(r))\neq y\}.

If ℰy\mathcal{E}_{y} occurs, then there must exist at least one competing label y′≠yy^{\prime}\neq y such that

log⁡π⁡(y′)+∑m,tlog⁡pm​(Xm,t∣y′)≥log⁡π⁡(y)+∑m,tlog⁡pm​(Xm,t∣y).\log\pi(y^{\prime})+\sum_{m,t}\log p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})\geq\log\pi(y)+\sum_{m,t}\log p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y).

Rearranging leads to

Δy,y′​(r)≥0.\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r)\geq 0.

Therefore,

ℰy⊆⋃y′∈𝒴∖{y}{Δy,y′(r)≥0}.\mathcal{E}_{y}\subseteq\bigcup_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{y\}}\{\Delta_{y,y^{\prime}}(r)\geq 0\}.

Apply the union bound. Taking conditional probabilities given Y=yY=y and applying the union bound allows (7). ∎

B.2 Proof of Proposition 1

The proof applies the exponential Markov inequality and evaluates the resulting moment via an auxiliary factorization lemma.

Lemma 2 (Exponential moment factorization).

For all distinct y,y′∈𝒴y,y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}, r∈ℤ≥0Kr\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{K}, and s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1],

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(s​∑m=1K∑t=1rmlog⁡pm​(Xm,t∣y′)pm​(Xm,t∣y))|Y=y]=∏m=1K(Mm(y,y′)​(s))rm.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\left(s\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{t=1}^{r_{m}}\log\frac{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})}{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)}\right)\middle|Y=y\right]=\prod_{m=1}^{K}\left(M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)\right)^{r_{m}}. (16)
Proof of Lemma 2.

Rewrite the exponent as

exp⁡(s​∑m=1K∑t=1rmlog⁡(pm​(Xm,t∣y′)pm​(Xm,t∣y)))\displaystyle\exp\!\left(s\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{t=1}^{r_{m}}\log\left(\frac{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})}{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)}\right)\right)
=∏m=1K∏t=1rm(pm​(Xm,t∣y′)pm​(Xm,t∣y))s=∏m=1K∏t=1rmpm​(Xm,t∣y)−s​pm​(Xm,t∣y′)s.\displaystyle\qquad=\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}\left(\frac{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})}{p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)}\right)^{s}=\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)^{-s}\,p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})^{s}.

Conditional on Y=yY=y the random variables {Xm,t}m,t\{X_{m,t}\}_{m,t} are independent across (m,t)(m,t), and for each fixed mm the repeats are i.i.d. with pm(⋅∣y)p_{m}(\cdot\mid y). Therefore, by the definition of independence,

𝔼⁡[∏m=1K∏t=1rmpm​(Xm,t∣y)−s​pm​(Xm,t∣y′)s|Y=y]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)^{-s}\,p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})^{s}\,\bigg|\,Y=y\right]
=∏m=1K∏t=1rm𝔼⁡[pm​(Xm,t∣y)−s​pm​(Xm,t∣y′)s|Y=y].\displaystyle\qquad=\prod_{m=1}^{K}\prod_{t=1}^{r_{m}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)^{-s}\,p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})^{s}\,\bigg|\,Y=y\right].

For any fixed (m,t)(m,t), conditional on Y=yY=y we have Pr⁡(Xm,t=x∣Y=y)=pm​(x∣y)\Pr(X_{m,t}=x\mid Y=y)=p_{m}(x\mid y), hence

𝔼⁡[pm​(Xm,t∣y)−s​pm​(Xm,t∣y′)s|Y=y]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y)^{-s}\,p_{m}(X_{m,t}\mid y^{\prime})^{s}\,\bigg|\,Y=y\right] =∑x∈𝒳mpm​(x∣y)​pm​(x∣y)−s​pm​(x∣y′)s\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{m}}p_{m}(x\mid y)\,p_{m}(x\mid y)^{-s}\,p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})^{s}
=∑x∈𝒳mpm​(x∣y) 1−s​pm​(x∣y′)s=Mm(y,y′)​(s),\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{m}}p_{m}(x\mid y)^{\,1-s}\,p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})^{\,s}=M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s),

where the last equality is (8). Since the same quantity appears for each t∈{1,…,rm}t\in\{1,\ldots,r_{m}\}, we obtain (16). ∎

We next establish basic analytic properties of the Chernoff affinity factor Mm(y,y′)​(s)M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s) used throughout the analysis.

Lemma 3 (Bounds on the Chernoff affinity factor).

Under Assumption 3.2, for all s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1],

0<Mm(y,y′)​(s)≤1.0<M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)\leq 1.

Moreover,

Mm(y,y′)​(0)=Mm(y,y′)​(1)=1.M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(0)=M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(1)=1.

For s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1), equality Mm(y,y′)​(s)=1M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)=1 holds if and only if pm(⋅∣y)=pm(⋅∣y′)p_{m}(\cdot\mid y)=p_{m}(\cdot\mid y^{\prime}).

Proof of Lemma 3.

Positivity. Under Assumption 3.2, each term

pm​(x∣y)1−s​pm​(x∣y′)sp_{m}(x\mid y)^{1-s}p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})^{s}

is strictly positive. Summing over the finite set 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} therefore gives Mm(y,y′)​(s)>0M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)>0.

Endpoint values. At s=0s=0,

Mm(y,y′)​(0)=∑x∈𝒳mpm​(x∣y)=1.M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(0)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{m}}p_{m}(x\mid y)=1.

At s=1s=1,

Mm(y,y′)​(1)=∑x∈𝒳mpm​(x∣y′)=1.M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(1)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{m}}p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})=1.

Upper bound for s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1) via Hölder’s inequality. Let

f⁡(x)=pm​(x∣y)1−s,g⁡(x)=pm​(x∣y′)s.f(x)=p_{m}(x\mid y)^{1-s},\qquad g(x)=p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})^{s}.

Choose conjugate exponents

p=11−s,q=1s.p=\frac{1}{1-s},\qquad q=\frac{1}{s}.

Applying Hölder’s inequality on the finite sum over 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} gives

∑xf⁡(x)​g​(x)≤(∑xf​(x)p)1/p​(∑xg​(x)q)1/q.\sum_{x}f(x)g(x)\leq\left(\sum_{x}f(x)^{p}\right)^{1/p}\left(\sum_{x}g(x)^{q}\right)^{1/q}.

f​(x)p=pm​(x∣y),g​(x)q=pm​(x∣y′),f(x)^{p}=p_{m}(x\mid y),\qquad g(x)^{q}=p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime}),

both sums equal 1 by normalization. Hence Mm(y,y′)​(s)≤1M_{m}^{(y,y^{\prime})}(s)\leq 1.

Equality condition. Hölder’s inequality is tight if and only if f​(x)pf(x)^{p} is proportional to g​(x)qg(x)^{q} for all xx. This requires

pm​(x∣y)=γ​pm​(x∣y′)p_{m}(x\mid y)=\gamma\,p_{m}(x\mid y^{\prime})

for some γ>0\gamma>0. Summing over xx gives γ=1\gamma=1, which implies pm(⋅∣y)=pm(⋅∣y′)p_{m}(\cdot\mid y)=p_{m}(\cdot\mid y^{\prime}). ∎

Proof of Proposition 1.
